rows.speaker: معاذ بن جبل
rows.claim: A man of Banu Salama blamed Kaʿb's absence on vanity and fine clothes; Muʿadh rebuked him and testified that he knew only good of Kaʿb.
rows.anchor: فقال له معاذ بن جبل : بئسما قلت والله يا رسول الله ما علمنا عليه إلا خيرا

rows.speaker: كعب بن مالك
rows.claim: When he heard the Prophet was returning, Kaʿb considered inventing an excuse but recognized that lying could not save him and resolved to tell the truth.
rows.anchor: قد أظل قادما زاح عني الباطل وعرفت أني لم أنج منه بشيء أبدا

rows.speaker: كعب بن مالك
rows.claim: About eighty men offered excuses; the Prophet accepted their outward professions, sought forgiveness for them, and left their hidden intentions to God.
rows.anchor: وكانوا بضعة وثمانين رجلا فقبل رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم علانيتهم وإستغفر لهم ووكل سرائرهم إلى الله

rows.speaker: كعب بن مالك
rows.claim: Kaʿb confessed that he had no excuse and had been able to go; the Prophet affirmed his truthfulness and deferred judgment to God.
rows.anchor: والله ما كان لي عذر والله ما كنت قط أفرغ ولا أيسر مني حين تخلفت عنك

rows.speaker: كعب بن مالك
rows.claim: Two other truthful veterans of Badr, Marārah ibn al-Rabīʿ and Hilāl ibn Umayya, gave the same answer and shared Kaʿb's fate.
rows.anchor: مرارة بن الربيع وهلال بن أمية فذكروا لي رجلين صالحين قد شهدوا بدرا

rows.speaker: كعب بن مالك
rows.claim: The Prophet prohibited people from speaking to the three, and the estrangement lasted fifty nights, making the familiar earth feel alien to Kaʿb.
rows.anchor: ونهى رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم عن كلامنا أيها الثلاثة

rows.speaker: كعب بن مالك
rows.claim: During the boycott Kaʿb still attended prayer and walked the markets, but nobody spoke to him; he watched for a response from the Prophet.
rows.anchor: فكنت أشهد الصلاة مع المسلمين وأطوف بالأسواق فلا يكلمني أحد

rows.speaker: كعب بن مالك
rows.claim: The Prophet would turn toward Kaʿb while he prayed but turn away when Kaʿb looked at him.
rows.anchor: فإذا أقبلت علي صلاتي أقبل إلي فإذا إلتفت نحوه أعرض

rows.speaker: كعب بن مالك
rows.claim: Kaʿb repeatedly asked his cousin Abū Qatāda whether he knew Kaʿb loved God and His Messenger; Abū Qatāda replied that God and His Messenger knew best, and Kaʿb wept.
rows.anchor: هل تعلم أني أحب الله تعالى ورسوله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال : فسكت

rows.speaker: كعب بن مالك
rows.claim: A letter from the Ghassānī ruler invited Kaʿb to join him because the Prophet had supposedly cast him aside; Kaʿb treated the offer as another trial and burned it.
rows.anchor: أما بعد فقد بلغنا أن صاحبك قد جفاك ولم يجعلك الله تعالى بدار هوان ولا مضيعة فالحق بنا نواسيك

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: After forty days of the boycott, a messenger ordered Kaʿb and the other two to separate from their wives, clarifying that they need not divorce them but must not approach them.
rows.anchor: إن رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم يأمرك أن تعتزل إمرأتك قلت أطلقها أم ماذا أفعل قال بل إعتزلها ولا تقربها

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: The Prophet allowed Hilāl's elderly wife, who had no helper, to serve him, but forbade marital intimacy; she said Hilāl had wept continually.
rows.anchor: فقال : لا ولكن لا يقربنك قالت : وإنه والله ما به حركة إلى شيء

rows.speaker: كعب بن مالك
rows.claim: Kaʿb sent his wife to her family and refused to seek permission to keep her, uncertain how the Prophet would answer and mindful that he was young.
rows.anchor: إلحقي بأهلك لتكوني عندهم حتى يقضي الله تعالى في هذا الإمر

rows.speaker: كعب بن مالك
rows.claim: At dawn after the fiftieth night, while sitting in the distress described by the verse, Kaʿb heard a caller on Mount Sal announce God's acceptance of their repentance and prostrated.
rows.anchor: سمعت صارخا أوفى على جبل سلع يقول بأعلى صوته : يا كعب بن مالك أبشر

rows.speaker: كعب بن مالك
rows.claim: People hurried to bring the news, and the caller's voice reached Kaʿb before the mounted messenger; Kaʿb gave the messenger the only two garments he owned and borrowed replacements.
rows.anchor: فكان الصوت أسرع من الفرس فلما جاءني الذي سمعت صوته يبشرني نزعت له ثوبي وكسوتهما إياه ببشارته

rows.speaker: كعب بن مالك
rows.claim: Ṭalḥa ibn ʿUbayd Allāh alone among the Emigrants rose, hurried to greet Kaʿb, and congratulated him; Kaʿb never forgot this kindness.
rows.anchor: فقام إلي طلحة بن عبيد الله يهرول حتى صافحني وهنأني والله ما قام إلي رجل من المهاجرين غيره

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: The Prophet told Kaʿb this was the best day of his life since his mother bore him, and clarified that the good news came from God.
rows.anchor: قال : لا بل من عند الله تعالى وكان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم إذا سر

rows.speaker: كعب بن مالك
rows.claim: Kaʿb offered to give all his wealth in charity as repentance, but the Prophet advised him to keep some; he retained his share at Khaybar.
rows.anchor: قال : أمسك بعض مالك فهو خير لك قلت : إني أمسك سهمي الذي بخيبر

rows.speaker: كعب بن مالك
rows.claim: Kaʿb resolved to speak only truth for the rest of his life, credited truthful confession with his salvation, and said he had not deliberately lied since making that vow.
rows.anchor: إنما نجاني الله تعالى بالصدق وإن من توبتي أن لاأحدث إلا صدقا ما بقيت

rows.speaker: كعب بن مالك
rows.claim: Kaʿb says the verse of their repentance was revealed and regards his truthful answer as a greater blessing than anything received after Islam, unlike those who lied.
rows.anchor: فوالله ما أنعم الله تعالى علي من نعمة قط بعد أن هداني الله سبحانه للإسلام عظم في نفسي من صدقي رسول الله

rows.speaker: كعب بن مالك
rows.claim: In another account Kaʿb feared dying ostracized or outliving the Prophet in permanent isolation; Umm Salama advocated for him, and the Prophet announced their pardon after dawn prayer to spare them a sleepless crowd.
rows.anchor: وما من شيء أهم إلي من أن أموت فلا يصلي علي رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description of the three's distress demonstrates the strength of their faith and the sincerity of their repentance.
rows.anchor: دلالة وأية دلالة على قوة إيمانهم وصدق توبتهم

rows.speaker: أبو بكر الوراق
rows.claim: Al-Warrāq defines sincere repentance through the constriction of the repentant person's world and soul, exemplified by Kaʿb and his two companions.
rows.anchor: أن تضيق على التائب الأرض بما رحبت وتضيق عليه نفسه كتوبة كعب ابن مالك وصاحبيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening simile introduces the fleeting enjoyment of worldly life and the rapid disappearance of its pleasures after people are drawn in by its flourishing.
rows.anchor: كلام مستأنف لبيان شأن الحياة الدنيا وقصر مدة التمتع فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A parable transfers an unusual or wondrous matter from its source to what it illustrates; here the comparison depicts worldly life quickly passing away.
rows.anchor: وأصل المثل ما شبه مضربه بمورده يستعار للأمر العجيب المستغرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The water causes the earth's vegetation to grow densely and intertwine; Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation supports this causal reading, though others take the water as accompanying the vegetation.
rows.anchor: فالباء للسببية ومنهممن أبقاها على المصاحبة وجعل الإختلاط بالماء نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about what people and livestock eat is circumstantial and refers to crops, vegetables, grasses, and pasture.
rows.anchor: كالبقول والزروع والحشيش والمراعي والجار والمجرور في موضع الحال من النبات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Several commentators construe the adorned earth as a bride: the bride is an implied metaphor, taking adornment is its imaginative completion, and the following wording extends it.
rows.anchor: ذكر غير واحد أن في الكلام إستعارة بالكناية حيث شبهت الأرض بالعروس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation takes the earth's adornment as gold, metaphorically describing its freshness and pleasing appearance.
rows.anchor: وقيل : الزخرف الذهب أستعير للنضارة والمنظر الشار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The standard form derives from tazayyanat by assimilation of tāʾ into zāy and an added connecting hamza; several variant readings preserve or reshape the form.
rows.anchor: وأصل ازينت تزينت فأدغمت التاء في الزاي وسكنت فإجتلبت همزة وصل

rows.speaker: عبدالله
rows.claim: ʿAbd Allāh reads the underlying form تزينت before assimilation.
rows.anchor: وبالأصل قرأ عبدالله

rows.speaker: الأعرج والشعبي وأبو العالية ونصر بن عاصم والحسن
rows.claim: These readers, with disagreement from al-Ḥasan, transmit the form أرينت on the pattern of afʿalat.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعرج والشعبي وأبو العالية ونصر بن عاصم والحسن بخلاف ( وأرينت ) بوزن أفعلت

rows.speaker: أبو عثمان النهدي
rows.claim: Abū ʿUthmān al-Nahdī reads ازيأنت with a hamza after the initial connecting hamza.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عثمان النهدي ( ازيأنت ) بهمزة وصل بعدها زاي ساكنة

rows.speaker: عوف بن جميل
rows.claim: ʿAwf ibn Jamīl reads ازيانت without replacing the alif with hamza; another reading intensifies the form as ازاينت.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عوف بن جميل ( ازيانت ) بألف من غير إبدال وقريء ( ازاينت ) لقصد المبالغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verbal forms here indicate becoming adorned, either by acquiring beauty or by adorning oneself.
rows.anchor: ومعنى الأفعال هنال هنا الصيرورة أي صارت ذات زينة أو صيرت نفسها كذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The owners think they can use the earth, obtain its fruit, and harvest its yields; the coming divine command then strikes its crops with destructive calamities.
rows.anchor: والمراد ظنوا أنهم متمكنون من منفعتها محصلون لثمرتهارافعون لغلتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The punishment can arrive by night or day: neither their heedlessness nor their wakefulness prevents it, and no defender can avert it.
rows.anchor: لا فرق في إتيان العذاب بين زمن غفلتهم وزمن يقظتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The harvested field is an explicit simile for the ruined vegetation; a direct metaphor is also possible, but al-Sakkākī's implied metaphor in which the embellished earth is the thriving plant is remote.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن هذا من التشبيه لذكر الطرفين فيه

rows.speaker: السكّاكي
rows.claim: Al-Sakkākī reads the passage as an implied metaphor, with the harvest image functioning as imaginative elaboration; al-Ālūsī finds this reading strained.
rows.anchor: وذهب السكاكي إلى أن في الكلام إستعارة بالكناية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb تغن means that the plant did not remain or dwell there; the omitted possessive makes the earth itself seem harvested and then unchanged, intensifying the image.
rows.anchor: أي لم يمكث ولم يقم فتغن من غني بالمكان إذا أقام ومكث فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronouns are best referred throughout to the earth, with ellipsis; on al-Ḥasan's masculine reading يغني, however, the subject must be vegetation or crops.
rows.anchor: وأنت تعلم أن إرجاع الضمائر كلها للأرض ولومع إرتكاب التجوز في الإسناد أولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yesterday is an idiom for a recent time before the event; the simile can be circumstantial or an independent answer to an implied question.
rows.anchor: أي فيما قبل إتيان أمرنا بزمان قريب فإن الأمس مثل في ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The composite comparison is the sudden disappearance of lush, intertwined vegetation after people expect it to escape disaster, not the rain itself.
rows.anchor: والممثل به في الآية ما يفهم من الكلام وهو زوال خضرة النبات فجأة

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: A reading attributed to Ubayy adds that God destroyed the land only because of its people's sins.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي أنه قرأ ( كأن لم تغن بالأمس وما أهلكناها إلا بذنوب أهلها )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verses being set out are Quranic signs, which are clarified for reflective people because they benefit from them; alternatively, the signs are the created events in the parable.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي مجلز أنه قال : كان مكتوبا إلى جنب هذه الآية فمحي

rows.speaker: أبو مجلز
rows.claim: Abū Mijlaz says a saying about Adam's child wanting a third valley of wealth and being filled only by earth was written beside this verse, then erased.
rows.anchor: كان مكتوبا إلى جنب هذه الآية فمحي ( ولو أن لإبن آدم واديين من مال لتمنى واديا ثالثا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in the claim that the owners could control it is understood as the earth; alternative referents are crops, fruit, or adornment.
rows.anchor: الكناية للزروع وقيل : للثمرة وقيل : للزينة لإنفهام ذلك من الكلام

rows.speaker: حمزة
rows.claim: Ḥamza reads يحشرهم with yāʾ; the other readers use the first-person plural, shifting to direct address.
rows.anchor: وهي قراءة حمزة على عاصم وقرأ الباقون بالنون على الإلتفات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most grammarians take يوم as an object of an omitted command to remember or warn them of the day of gathering for judgment.
rows.anchor: عند الأكثرين منصوب بمضمر أي أذكر لهم أو أنذرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hour of a day is proverbial for an extremely short time; daytime is specified because its hours are more familiar than nighttime hours.
rows.anchor: فإنها مثل في غاية القلة وتخصيصها بالنهار لأن ساعاته أعرف حالا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The simile is a circumstantial description of the gathered people, as if their stay in worldly life or the barzakh had been only brief.
rows.anchor: والجملة في موقع الحال منمفعول ( نحشرهم )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The comparison chiefly expresses regret at wasting their lives or wishing they had remained longer before witnessing the terrors; reading it literally is less persuasive.
rows.anchor: فالمراد إما التأسف على عدم إنتفاعهم بأعمارهم أو تمنى أن يطول مكثهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some preserve the literal comparison by saying long-lived people would retain signs of worldly prosperity, but al-Ālūsī calls this an artificial reading.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه تكلف لإبقاء التشبيه على ظاهره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the brief stay refers to the barzakh, it can show resurrection's ease despite its duration and answer their denial, or indicate that forms remain unchanged after a short interval.
rows.anchor: بيان كمال يسر الحشر بالنسبة إلى قدرته تعالى

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī allows the clause to describe the Day or an omitted noun for resurrection, but objections concern its deleted link and definiteness; al-Ālūsī favors the circumstantial reading.
rows.anchor: وجوز أبو علي كون الجملة في موضع الصفة ليوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause about mutual recognition either resumes the account or explains the brief-stay comparison; the inference from recognition to short duration is not conclusive.
rows.anchor: يحتمل أن يكون إستئنافا وأن يكون بيانا للجملة التشبيهية

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ calls recognition a prospective circumstantial clause, but al-Ālūsī sees no need to suppose a delay after resurrection.
rows.anchor: وزعم أبو البقاء كونه حالا مقدرة ولا داعي لإعتبار كونها مقدرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Recognition occurs on first emerging from the graves, then may cease amid terror; al-Ālūsī adds that different scenes could allow renewed recognition after estrangement.
rows.anchor: ما يؤيد ذلك وزعم بعضهم المنافاة بين ما تدل عليه هذه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some commentators allege a conflict between recognition and verses denying kinship and mutual questioning.
rows.anchor: وزعم بعضهم المنافاة بين ما تدل عليه هذه الآية وما يدل عليه قوله سبحانه : ( لا أنساب بينهم يومئذ ولا يتساءلون )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that the deniers lost is best read as God's independent testimony to their loss, though some make it quoted speech or a circumstantial clause.
rows.anchor: جملة مستأنفة سيقت للشهادة منه تعالى على خسرانهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording identifies them as those who denied meeting God to condemn them by the trait that caused their fate; meeting means reckoning and recompense, and loss is failed spiritual commerce.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن المراد بلقاء الله تعالى مطلق الحساب والجزاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative takes meeting as a bad encounter and loss as ruin and misguidance.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يراد بالأول سوء اللقاءو بالثاني الهلاك والضلال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They were not guided either in the figurative trade of salvation or toward the road to safety; the final clause coordinates with the loss statement or reinforces the relative clause.
rows.anchor: أي لطرق التجارة عارفين بأحوالها وما كانوامهتدين إلى طريق النجاة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says a person recognizes the neighbor beside him but cannot speak to him.
rows.anchor: فقد أخرج ابن أبي حاتم وأبو الشيخ عن الحسن أنه قال فيها : يعرف الرجل صاحبه إلى جنبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taking recognition to mean that people identify one another's past error and disbelief is an unsupported interpretation.
rows.anchor: وقيل : المراد به التعريف أي يعرف بعضهم بعضا ما كانوا من الخطأ والكفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet cannot control harm or benefit; harm comes first because the passage stresses inability to bring punishment, while benefit completes the expression of total helplessness.
rows.anchor: وتقديم الضر لما أن مساق النظم الكريم لإظهار العجز عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second explanation calls mention of benefit a digression to prevent readers from thinking incapacity applies only to harm; the order is reversed in al-Aʿrāf because benefit is then central.
rows.anchor: وقيل : إنهإستطرادي لئلا يتوهم إختصاص ذلك بالضر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disconnected-exception reading means that whatever God wills will occur; the connected reading means whatever He wills the Prophet to control.
rows.anchor: وقيل : متصل على معنى إلا ما شاء الله تعالى أن أملكه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Muʿtazilites use a connected exception to argue that people independently control their acts, but al-Ālūsī says the verse falls far short of proving this.
rows.anchor: والمعتزلة قالوا بإتصال الإستثناء وإستدلوا بذلك على أن العبد مستقل بأفعاله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some proponents of the Salaf's view infer that human capacity has an effect only by God's permission, between the Jabriyya denial of capacity, the common Ashʿarī denial of its efficacy, and the Muʿtazilī claim of independent effect.
rows.anchor: من أن للعبد قدرة مؤثرة بإذن الله تعالى لا أنه ليس له قدرة أصلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If ملك means ability, the exception is connected; if it retains literal ownership, it must be disconnected, though connection is the default whenever it works without strain.
rows.anchor: إذا كان الملك بمعنى الإستطاعة يكون الإستثناء متصلاوإذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second clause may prohibit both delay and advance; placing impossible advance beside delay intensifies the impossibility, and istifʿāl can suggest that even seeking it is inconceivable.
rows.anchor: وهذا هو السر في إيراد صيغة الإستفعال أي أنه بلغ في الإستحالة إلى أنه لا يطلب

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī treats denial of advancing or delaying as an idiom for a fixed, appointed limit, illustrated by a line from al-Ḥamāsa.
rows.anchor: وأشار الزمخشري إلى جواب آخر وهو أن لا يتأخر ولا يتقدم كناية عن كونه له حد معين

rows.speaker: المرزوقي
rows.claim: Al-Marzūqī explains the cited poem as the lover remaining with his beloved in every situation, whether she stays or departs.
rows.anchor: فإنه أراد كما قال المرزوقي حبسني الهوى في موضع تستقرين فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse is an independent part of the answer, and the order of denying delay before advance has already been discussed under al-Aʿrāf.
rows.anchor: ثم لا يخفى أن هذه الآية داخلة في حيز الجواب ولم تعطف على ما قبلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī rejects the claim that the exception shifts the subject from the Prophet to God, as though only God owns and does whatever He wills.
rows.anchor: ومما يقضي منه العجب زعم أن الإستثناء من فاعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Each community has a fixed time appointed for its punishment, which does not transfer to another community.
rows.anchor: لعذابهم يحل بهم عند حلوله لا يتعدى إلى أمة أخرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording specifies each community's own deadline; أجل can mean its fixed time limit, whose arrival means its completion, and ساعة denotes a tiny interval.
rows.anchor: إذا تم وإنقضى أجلهم الخاص بهم فلا يستأخرون عنه ساعة

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: Al-Ṭībī says the reply uses a wise redirection: the questioners mockingly demand a time, but the Prophet disavows control over even his own affairs before answering properly.
rows.anchor: وارد على الأسلوب الحكيم لأنهم ما أرادوا بالسؤال إلا إستعباد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The substantive answer is that God has fixed a time for the promised punishment, which will inevitably be fulfilled, so the people should not hasten it.
rows.anchor: عذابكم له أجل مضروب عند الله تعالى وحد محدود من الزمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī explains omission of fa before the deadline condition as presenting it as independently established, while the fa in the consequence strengthens the condition's necessary result.
rows.anchor: فأتي بها غير متفرعة على شيء كأنها من الأمور الثابتة في نفسها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relation to the preceding clause may clarify the exception and qualify the decree; this is a possible account of the sentence connection.
rows.anchor: قيل في ربط هذهالآية بما قبلها من أنها بيان لما أبهم

rows.speaker: صفاء الدين عيسى البندنيجي
rows.claim: Al-Bandhanījī says the passage consoles the Prophet against mockery: each clause stands independently for emphasis, unlike al-Aʿrāf, which directly threatens Meccans and links the warning with fa.
rows.anchor: أن مساق هذه الآية لتثبيت النبي صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم وشرح صدره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī ridicules a grammarian's claim that the differing connective particles merely show two forms are both grammatically possible; the Quran's purpose is eloquence, not grammar instruction.
rows.anchor: ومما تضحك منه الموتى ما قاله بعض العظاميين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The interrogative آلآن rebukes Pharaoh for professing faith only after despairing of life; an omitted verb is estimated after the adverb to direct the reproach at the delay.
rows.anchor: الإستفهام للإنكار والتوبيخ والظرف متعلق بمحذوف يقدر مؤخرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rebuke is attributed variously to God, Gabriel, or Michael.
rows.anchor: والقائل له ذلك فقيل : هو الله تعالى وقيل : هو جبريل عليه السلام

rows.speaker: أبو أمامة
rows.claim: A report from Abū Umāma via Abū al-Shaykh says Gabriel hated Pharaoh, feared he might utter the confession and escape, put mud into his mouth, and that God became angrier than Gabriel.
rows.anchor: أخرج أبو الشيخ عن أبي أمامة قال : قال رسول الله

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī calls the report fabrications against God and the angels: a blocked mouth cannot prevent inward faith, and hating a disbeliever's faith would itself be unbelief; Ibn al-Munīr endorses his objection.
rows.anchor: وفي الكشاف أن ذلك من زيادات الباهتين لله تعالى وملائكته عليهم السلام

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report transmitted by several collectors and authenticated by al-Tirmidhī and al-Ḥākim has Gabriel say that he put sea mud into Pharaoh's mouth lest mercy reach him.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما قال : قال رسول الله تعالى

rows.speaker: إرشاد العقل السليم
rows.claim: Irshād construes mercy as worldly rescue, which need not entail valid faith, as in the case of Jonah's people; Gabriel merely closed off a remote possibility. Al-Ālūsī finds this reading unlikely.
rows.anchor: أن المراد بالرحمة الرحمة الدنيوية أي النجاة التي هي طلبة المخذول

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: A report from Abū Hurayra says Gabriel covered Pharaoh with one hand and put mud in his mouth fearing God's mercy might reach him and God forgive him; al-Ālūsī says this denotes forgiveness, not earthly rescue.
rows.anchor: عن أبي هريرة رضي الله تعالى عنه قال : قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: بعض المحققين
rows.claim: Another verifier explains Gabriel's act as anger and fear that repeated confession might, by extraordinary mercy, be accepted; he says approving one's own unbelief is unbelief, while disapproving another's is not necessarily so.
rows.anchor: إنما فعل جبريل عليه السلام ما فعل غضبا عليه لما صدر منه وخوفا أنه إذا كرر ذلك

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: Al-Ṭībī says sound transmitted reports should be accepted even when reason cannot explain them, with the limitation assigned to the reader.
rows.anchor: ليس للعقل مجال في مثل هذا النقل الصحيح إلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī counters that if a report contradicts clear reason or attributes an impossible defect to an infallible angel and admits no sound interpretation, doubt should fall on its transmitter rather than reason.
rows.anchor: وإتهام الراوي بما يوهن أمر روايته أهون من إتهام العقل الصريح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase وقد عصيت قبل is a circumstantial clause intensifying the rebuke: Pharaoh delayed faith without excuse, while his corruption also harmed others through oppression and blocking Israel's way.
rows.anchor: في موضع الحال من فاعل الفعل العامل في الظرف

rows.speaker: الكسائي ويعقوب
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī and Yaʿqūb read ننجي with a light jīm; the standard reading doubles it.
rows.anchor: بالتشديد وعن الكسائي ويعقوب بالتخفيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rescue clause follows an implied statement that earlier nations were destroyed; the intervening text hastens the threat, and this passage narrates destruction before rescue.
rows.anchor: يدل عليه قول سبحانه : ( مثل أيام الذين خلوا ) وما بينهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The present-tense rescue vividly recounts a past event; believers are saved as in prior instances, and the concluding sentence reaffirms this outcome.
rows.anchor: وعبر بالمضارع لحكاية الحال الماضية لتهويل أمرها بإستحضار صورها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: That rescue is a sure divine promise, termed obligatory only figuratively, since nothing truly imposes an obligation on God.
rows.anchor: ومعنى كون الإنجاء واجبا أنه كالأمر الواجب عليه تعالى وإلا فلا وجوب حقيقة عليه سبحانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers may mean all believers, including messengers and followers, or only followers; messengers are omitted in the latter reading because they were already named.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالمؤمنين إما الجنس المتناول للرسل عليهم السلام وأتباعهم وأما الأتباع فقط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The concluding clause teaches that faith is the basis of rescue and seals the preceding statement by reaffirming its meaning.
rows.anchor: ففيه تنبيه على أن مدار الإنجاء هو الإيمان وجيء بهذه الجملة تذييلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse describes those whose good-looking deeds seek worldly life and its adornments, such as health, security, wealth, children, and status, with كَان suggesting persistent intent and little concern for the afterlife.
rows.anchor: أي ما يزينها ويحسنها من الصحة والأمن وكثرة الأموال والأولاد والرياسة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They receive the full recompense of their deeds in this life; the phrase omits a genitive meaning their rewards, rather than using deeds metaphorically for rewards.
rows.anchor: فالكلام على حذف مضاف وقيل : الأعمال عبارة عن الأجور مجازا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb نوف includes the sense of conveying, which explains its construction with إلى even though it normally takes a direct object.
rows.anchor: متضمن معنى نوصل ولذا عدى بإلى وإلا

rows.speaker: طلحة بن ميمون
rows.claim: Ṭalḥa ibn Maymūn reads يوف with yāʾ and the verb attributed to God; Zayd ibn ʿAlī uses a light form, and a passive reading raises أعمالهم.
rows.anchor: وقرأ طلحة بن ميمون يوف بالياء وإسناد الفعل إلى الله تعالى

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan reads نوفي without the final yāʾ in the jussive, explained through Arabic deletion patterns or the weakened force of a distant conditional response.
rows.anchor: ونقل عن عبدالقاهر أنها لا تعمل فيه أصلا لضعفها

rows.speaker: الفَرّاء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says كان is extra and accounts for the jussive response; Abū Ḥayyān objects that the actual conditional verb يريد would then have to be jussive.
rows.anchor: وحكى الفراء أن ( كان ) زائدة ولذا جزم الجواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: لا يبخسون means their worldly recompense is not reduced; the pronoun most naturally refers to worldly life, though another view refers it to the deeds.
rows.anchor: وقيل : الأظهر أن يكون للأعمال لئلا يكون تكرارا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording presents full recompense as payment of a right and non-reduction as avoiding injustice, although the recipients have no claim to it; the promise remains governed by God's wise will.
rows.anchor: بل الأمر دائر على المشيئة الجارية على قضية الحكمة

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Rāghib defines bakhs as an unjust reduction, which heightens the denial of any shortfall.
rows.anchor: ولذلك قال الراغب : هو نقص الشيء على سبيل الظلم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās is quoted by al-Naḥḥās as saying that the verse of worldly recompense abrogated the present verse; al-Ālūsī says abrogation of reports is impossible and treats the statement as loose usage.
rows.anchor: وأخرج النحاس في ناسخه عن ابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما أن هذه الآية نسخت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demonstrative may refer to persistent worldly intent, full recompense in this life, or both; its distance signals how far the people are from goodness.
rows.anchor: إشارة إلى المذكورين باعتبار استمرارهم على إرادة الحياة الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They have only Hell in the afterlife because their aims and actions were confined to worldly acquisition, whose reward they already received.
rows.anchor: لأن هممهم كانت مصروفة إلى اقتناص الدنيا وأعمالهم كانت ممدودة ومقصورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the apparent reading, their deeds are shown to have come to nothing in the afterlife; ما may be a verbal noun or refer to the deeds that could have earned afterlife reward.
rows.anchor: كما هو الظاهر فالجار متعلق بحبط و ( ما ) تحتمل المصدرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, فيها can refer to worldly life, describing the failure of their works through lack of sincerity or their having been rewarded in this world.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يعود الضمير إلى الدنيا فيكون الجار متعلقا بصنعوا

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān takes the final sentence as emphasis of the preceding claim that their works came to nothing.
rows.anchor: قال أبو حيان : هو تأكيد لقوله سبحانه : ( حبط ) إلخ

rows.speaker: أبو السعود
rows.claim: Abū al-Suʿūd distinguishes their outwardly good works, which fail to earn reward for lack of faith or right intention, from worldly pursuits intrinsically without lasting benefit; al-Ālūsī prefers this account.
rows.anchor: والأولى ما صنعه المولى أبو السعود عليه الرحمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī offers, but regards as unlikely, reading ما كانوا يعملون as their continuing desire for worldly life itself, a work of the heart.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل عندي على بعد أن يراد بما كانوا يعملون هو ما استمروا عليه من إرادة الحياة الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The normal syntax makes باطل a fronted predicate and ما كانوا يعملون its subject; other grammatical parses and the verbal reading بطل are also reported.
rows.anchor: فالظاهر أن ( باطل ) خبر مقدم و ( ما كانوا ) هو المبتدأ

rows.speaker: أبي وابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ubayy and Ibn Masʿūd read باطلا in the accusative, with several possible grammatical explanations for the construction.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبي وابن مسعود وباطلا بالنصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse applies generally to unbelievers whose good works lack the orientation required for afterlife reward; Jews and Christians may be occasions of revelation without being its exclusive subject.
rows.anchor: الآية في مطلق الكفرة الذين يعملون البر لا على الوجه الذي ينبغي

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: A report from Anas says the verse was revealed about Jews and Christians; Ibn ʿAṭiyya treats them as a cause of revelation included within a general rule.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن جرير وابن أبي حاتم وغيرهما عن أنس رضي الله تعالى عنه أنها نزلت في اليهود والنصارى

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī applies the verse to hypocrites who fought with the Prophet and received booty, but al-Ālūsī objects that the Meccan verse preceded that event.
rows.anchor: وقال الجبائي : هي في الذين جاهدوا من المنافقين مع رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some apply the verse to ostentatious worshippers, citing the report that a reciter, giver, or fallen fighter seeking reputation is told that he has received it but no divine reward; Muʿāwiya wept at the citation.
rows.anchor: يقال لقاريء القرآن منهم : أردت أن يقال : فلأن قاريء فقد قيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unbelievers commonly receive worldly recompense through health, wealth, and children; some scholars say good deeds lessen their afterlife punishment, while others deny benefit where intention is a condition, reconciling the evidence this way.
rows.anchor: ومن هنا اشتهر أن الكافر يجعل له ثواب أعماله في الدنيا بتوسعة الرزق وصحة البدن

rows.speaker: مجمع البيان
rows.claim: Majmaʿ al-Bayān connects the passage to the earlier question Will you submit?: if people profess Islam to protect life and property, this verse explains the result.
rows.anchor: أنه سبحانه لما قال : ( فهل أنتم مسلمون ) فكأن قائلا قال : إن أظهرنا الإسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another proposed link is that unbelievers might profess Islam or do good works in hopes of protection after hearing that their idols cannot save them; al-Ālūsī notes the account assumes such a precautionary intent.
rows.anchor: ذلك سببا لعزمهم على إظهار الإسلام أو فعل بعض الأعمال الصالحة

rows.speaker: البحر
rows.claim: Al-Baḥr relates the verse to the preceding discussion by adding the unbelievers' worldly circumstances and their ultimate afterlife outcome.
rows.anchor: وفي البحر في بيان المناسبة أنه سبحانه لما ذكر شيئا من أحوال الكفار في القرآن

rows.speaker: أبو السعود
rows.claim: Abū al-Suʿūd says the passage addresses unbelievers generally, especially Quranic critics: their apparent worldly gains do not show that they possess truth or anything substantial.
rows.anchor: أن المراد مطلق الكفرة بحيث يندرج فيهم القادحون في القرآن العظيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse is cited against charging for acts whose proper purpose is devotion; al-Kiyā al-Ṭabarī also invokes it for intention-dependent fasting and ablution, a disputed legal inference.
rows.anchor: واستدل في الأحكام بالآية على أن ما سبيله أن لا يفعل إلا على وجه القربة لا يجوز أخذ الأجرة عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah's son plans to climb a mountain, mistakenly treating the divinely sent flood as ordinary waters from which elevation could protect him.
rows.anchor: قال ذلك زعما منه أن ذلك كسائر المياه في أزمنة السيول المعتادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah's لا عاصم denies every possible protector, emphasizing that the mountain cannot save anyone from God's punishment; اليوم distinguishes this event from ordinary calamities where natural means can help.
rows.anchor: نفي لجنس العاصم المنتظم لنفي جميع أفراده ذاتا وصفة للمبالغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the flood أمر الله instead of repeating ماء magnifies the punishment, corrects the son's mistaken description, and establishes that only God's mercy can grant protection.
rows.anchor: وعبر عن الماء في محل إضماره بأمر الله أي عذابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The strongest interpretation makes rescue by divine mercy the exception, redirecting Noah's concern for his son toward God as the true refuge.
rows.anchor: وهو أحد أوجه في الآية وأقواها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second view treats عاصم as a rare relational form, so that the exception means no possessor of protection or protected person exists except one shown mercy; a passive reading supports this.
rows.anchor: الوجه الثاني أن عاصما صيغة نسبة والمراد بالموصول المرحوم
